examples.question_text: An enlargement multiplies every side of a figure by $1.8$ and leaves every angle unchanged. Is the enlarged figure similar to the original? Must similar figures have the same size?
examples.solution_text:
Corresponding angles are equal and every corresponding-side ratio is $1.8$, so the figures are similar.

Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size.

To the nearest degree, the remaining angle in each triangle is

$\begin{aligned}x&=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-23^{\circ}\\&=67^{\circ}.\end{aligned}$

The corresponding angles are equal. Compare larger sides with smaller sides:

$\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{12}&=1.5\\\frac{7.5}{5}&=1.5\\\frac{19.5}{13}&=1.5.\end{aligned}$

Every corresponding-side ratio is $1.5$, so the triangles are similar.

$\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{8}&=1.5\\\frac{8}{4}&=2.\end{aligned}$

All corresponding angles are $90^{\circ}$, but the corresponding-side ratios differ. The rectangles are not similar.

Equal corresponding angles alone do not guarantee similarity of polygons; corresponding sides must also be in the same ratio.

$\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{6}&=2\\\frac{10}{5}&=2\\\frac{10}{5}&=2\\\frac{6}{4}&=1.5\\\frac{6}{4}&=1.5.\end{aligned}$

The corresponding-side ratios are not all equal. The pentagons are not similar, even though their corresponding angles are equal.

Rectangle $A$ has long side $4$ units and short side $2$ units. Rectangle $B$ has long side $8$ units and short side $4$ units.

Match long sides with long sides and short sides with short sides:

$\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{4}&=2\\\frac{4}{2}&=2.\end{aligned}$

Corresponding angles are right angles and both ratios equal $2$, so the rectangles are similar. Rotation does not change shape.

Compare the bases and perpendicular heights:

$\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{4}&=1.5\\\frac{3}{3}&=1.\end{aligned}$

The base has increased by a factor of $1.5$, but the height is unchanged. An enlargement multiplies every length by the same factor, so the triangles are not similar. The student is incorrect.

examples.question_text:
Justify each statement.

(a) Any two squares are similar.

(b) Any two equilateral triangles are similar.

(c) Any two circles are similar.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Every square has four $90^{\circ}$ angles. If the side lengths of two squares are $a$ and $b$, every corresponding-side ratio is $\frac{b}{a}$. Both similarity properties hold.

(b) Every equilateral triangle has three $60^{\circ}$ angles. If their side lengths are $p$ and $q$, every corresponding-side ratio is $\frac{q}{p}$. Both similarity properties hold.

(c) A circle of radius $r$ can be enlarged or reduced to a circle of radius $s$ by multiplying every length by $\frac{s}{r}$. The shape is unchanged, so any two circles are similar.

coverage.summary: Authored seven worked examples covering the six distinct assessed methods using supplied booklet teaching and exercises. Practice and quiz content was preserved without repeating its audit. Examples have separate editable prompts and solutions, single-dollar mathematics, aligned calculations and unshaded native diagrams with black 10 pt labels. Solution prose and mathematics inherit the renderer’s blue. Final capture and independent example review remain coordinator stages.

examples.derivation: Unchanged corresponding angles and a common side ratio of 1.8 establish similarity. The enlargement changes size while preserving shape.

Both triangles are right triangles: 5²+12²=13² and 7.5²+18²=19.5². Their acute angles round to 23° and 67°. The corresponding-side ratios 18/12, 7.5/5 and 19.5/13 all equal 1.5. The diagram coordinates preserve these proportions.
The side ratios are 12/8=1.5 and 8/4=2. Although all angles are 90°, unequal corresponding-side ratios rule out similarity. Both drawings agree with their stated dimensions.

The base and two roof-side ratios equal 2; both vertical-side ratios equal 1.5. Similarity therefore fails. The roof directions and vertical/horizontal edges preserve equal corresponding angles, and the coordinates consistently represent every labelled length.
Grid counting gives A dimensions 4 by 2 and B dimensions 4 by 8. Matching long sides and short sides gives 8/4=4/2=2. With right angles, the rectangles are similar after allowing rotation.

The bases measure 4 and 6 grid units, while both perpendicular heights measure 3 units. Their ratios are 1.5 and 1, so no uniform enlargement maps X to Y. Both triangles are isosceles as drawn, making this comparison sufficient to reject similarity.

Squares have matching 90° angles and one common side ratio b/a. Equilateral triangles have matching 60° angles and one common side ratio q/p. Positive circle radii r and s give a uniform enlargement or reduction factor s/r.

review.summary: All seven examples are mathematically correct, source-aligned and within scope. The mappings cover all six distinct assessed methods and include every required assessment locator exactly once. There are no existing examples to audit and no source exceptions are needed. Native diagrams preserve givens without exposing answers; equation gutters are appropriate, and solution prose/math can inherit the supplied blue renderer styling. Final-size rendering and label verification remain for the capture stage. Accepted practice and quiz mathematics were not re-audited.
